text:
Canal du Midi

The Canal du Midi is a 240-kilometre canal in southern France that links the Garonne at Toulouse to the Étang de Thau, a lagoon on the Mediterranean coast near Sète. Built between 1666 and 1681 during the reign of Louis XIV, it is regarded as one of the most remarkable feats of civil engineering of the seventeenth century. Together with the Canal de Garonne, completed in 1856, it forms the Canal des Deux Mers, a continuous inland waterway between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. The canal was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996.

Name
At its opening the waterway was called the Canal royal en Languedoc. During the French Revolution, when royal names fell out of favour, it was renamed Canal du Midi, the name by which it has been known ever since. Locally it is often simply called "le canal".

History

Early proposals
The idea of joining the two seas across the narrow isthmus of southern France is ancient. Roman engineers are said to have considered it, and the project was studied again under Francis I and Henry IV. Each time it foundered on the same problem: a canal crossing the watershed between the Atlantic and Mediterranean basins needs a reliable supply of water at its highest point, and no one could find a way to bring enough water to the summit near the Seuil de Naurouze.

Riquet's project
The solution came from Pierre-Paul Riquet, a tax farmer from Béziers who had no formal training as an engineer but knew the Montagne Noire, the hills north of the watershed, intimately. Riquet realised that streams flowing down from the Montagne Noire could be captured and diverted along an artificial channel to the summit level. After years of surveying, he built a small trial channel on his own estate to demonstrate the principle. In 1666, Louis XIV's minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, who saw in the canal a way to avoid the long and dangerous sea route around Spain and to bypass the Strait of Gibraltar, persuaded the king to approve the project by royal edict.

Construction
Work began in 1667. At its height, the construction employed around 12,000 workers, including a large number of women, which was unusual for the time. Riquet introduced practices that were advanced for the period: workers were paid a regular monthly wage, including on rainy days and Sundays, and received sick pay, which helped him retain a skilled workforce over many years.

Financing was a constant struggle. The crown paid for part of the work, the provincial estates of Languedoc contributed, and Riquet invested his own fortune, much of which he lost. He died in October 1680, just months before the canal was completed. It was formally opened on 15 May 1681, and his sons finished the remaining works.

Later developments
The canal was soon found to need improvements. Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban, the military engineer, inspected it in 1686 and recommended a series of works, including additional aqueducts to carry the canal over streams that had previously flowed straight into it, bringing silt and floods. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the canal was extended by branches to Narbonne and to the port of La Nouvelle, and the Canal de Garonne was finally built to replace the unreliable river navigation between Toulouse and Bordeaux.

Engineering

Water supply
The heart of Riquet's design is the system that feeds the summit pound at the Seuil de Naurouze. Water is collected from streams in the Montagne Noire by a channel called the Rigole de la Montagne, then stored in the Bassin de Saint-Ferréol, a reservoir created by an earth dam that was, at the time of its completion, the largest dam in the world. A second channel, the Rigole de la Plaine, carries the water to the summit, where it is divided between the two slopes. An octagonal basin at Naurouze originally distributed the flow; it silted up and was later replaced by other arrangements.

Locks
The canal climbs from Toulouse to the summit and then descends to the Mediterranean through a series of locks. Their chambers are oval rather than rectangular, a shape chosen because early straight-walled chambers collapsed under the pressure of the surrounding earth; the curved walls act like an arch. The best-known structure is the staircase of Fonserannes near Béziers, where a series of linked chambers lifts boats about 21 metres over a short distance. A water slope built nearby in the 1980s to bypass the staircase is no longer in service.

Aqueducts, bridges and the Malpas tunnel
More than 300 structures, including locks, bridges, aqueducts, spillways and tunnels, were built along the canal. Near Béziers, the canal crosses the Orb river on an aqueduct completed in 1858, replacing a dangerous level crossing of the river itself. The Malpas tunnel, cut through a hill near Ensérune, was the first tunnel ever built for a navigable canal. Riquet reportedly ordered work to continue despite advice that the rock was too unstable, and the tunnel was lined with masonry in later centuries.

Economic role and decline
For nearly two centuries the canal was an important commercial artery. Barges carried wheat, wine, olive oil, textiles and building materials, while passenger boats offered a regular service between Toulouse and Agde. The canal stimulated the agricultural economy of Languedoc, particularly the trade in grain and later in wine.

The arrival of the railway in the mid-nineteenth century marked the beginning of its decline. In 1858 the operation of the canal was leased to the Compagnie des chemins de fer du Midi, the railway company that was its direct competitor, which raised tolls and favoured its own trains. Although the state bought back the lease in 1898 and abolished tolls, freight traffic never recovered. Commercial transport dwindled through the twentieth century and had all but disappeared by the end of the 1980s.

The plane trees
The canal is lined for much of its length by tens of thousands of trees, most of them plane trees planted in the nineteenth century to stabilise the banks and shade the towpath. Since 2006, the trees have been affected by canker stain, a fungal disease caused by Ceratocystis platani, which is believed to have arrived in southern France on wooden crates during the Second World War. There is no cure, and infected trees must be felled and burned to slow the spread. Voies navigables de France, the public body that manages the canal, launched a long-term programme to cut down affected trees and replant with disease-resistant species, including a hybrid plane tree variety, oaks, limes and poplars. The programme is expected to last for decades and is funded partly by public money and partly by donations.

Tourism today
Today the Canal du Midi is primarily a leisure waterway. Rental companies offer cabin cruisers that can be hired without a licence after a short briefing, and many visitors spend a week travelling a section of the canal at walking pace. The towpath has been progressively improved for cycling, notably between Toulouse and the Seuil de Naurouze and between Béziers and the coast. Popular stops include Castelnaudary, known for cassoulet; Carcassonne, whose medieval fortified city stands a short walk from the canal port; the village of Le Somail with its old barge stop; and the Fonserannes staircase.

Navigation is normally closed for several weeks in winter, when sections are drained for maintenance of locks and banks. Water shortages in hot, dry summers have occasionally forced managers to restrict lock operations.

Cultural significance
The canal has been celebrated by writers and painters since the seventeenth century. Thomas Jefferson travelled along it in 1787 while serving as American minister to France and wrote admiringly of its engineering. It appears in songs, regional literature and countless travel guides. For many residents of the region, the canal is less a monument than a familiar landscape: a place for a Sunday walk, a cycling route to work, or a fishing spot shaded by the remaining plane trees.

Statue and memorials
A statue of Pierre-Paul Riquet stands on the Allées Paul-Riquet in Béziers, his home town, and another overlooks the canal in Toulouse. His descendants owned a share of the canal until the nineteenth century. An obelisk erected at the Seuil de Naurouze in his honour marks the point where the waters divide between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.

Weeknight Shakshuka (Serves 4)

Prep 10 min · Cook 25 min · Vegetarian

This is the version I make when the fridge is nearly empty. It forgives a lot: swap the bell pepper for a courgette, use canned cherry tomatoes, or leave out the feta if you are cooking for someone dairy-free.

Ingredients
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 medium onion, thinly sliced
- 1 red bell pepper, diced
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tsp ground cumin, 1 tsp sweet paprika, a pinch of chili flakes
- 2 cans (400 g each) crushed tomatoes
- 1 tsp sugar (optional, only if your tomatoes taste sharp)
- 6 eggs
- 60 g feta, crumbled
- A handful of parsley or cilantro, chopped

Method
1. Heat the oil in a 28 cm skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and pepper and cook for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft but not browned.
2. Stir in the garlic and spices. Cook for one minute until fragrant. Do not let the garlic burn; if it starts to color, pull the pan off the heat.
3. Pour in the tomatoes, add the sugar if using, and season with salt. Simmer for 10 minutes until the sauce thickens enough that a spoon leaves a trail.
4. Make six wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each one. Cover the pan.
5. Cook for 5 to 7 minutes. Check after five: the whites should be set and the yolks still wobble when you shake the pan.
6. Remove from the heat, scatter the feta and herbs over the top, and serve straight from the skillet with crusty bread.

Tip: ignore recipes that tell you to bake it in the oven unless your skillet is very wide. On the stove you can see exactly when to stop.

text:
Why "Just Tell the Model to Be Careful" Doesn't Stop Prompt Injection

Large language models now read email, browse the web and open files on our behalf. That convenience creates a new security problem. When a model processes text written by someone else, that text can contain sentences crafted to look like commands. Security researchers call this prompt injection, and it is fundamentally different from the bugs we are used to.

In a classic SQL injection, the database receives a query in which data and code have been mixed together. The fix, parameterized queries, works because the database has a formal grammar: it can always tell where the data starts. A language model has no such grammar. Everything it reads, whether it came from the developer, the user or a random web page, arrives as one stream of tokens. The model has learned that some parts of the stream carry more authority than others, but that boundary is statistical, not enforced.

That is why the obvious mitigation, adding a line to the system prompt asking the model to disregard instructions found in documents, only reduces the success rate. A sufficiently persuasive passage can still win.

What works better is limiting what a successful attack can achieve:

- Least privilege. An assistant that summarizes web pages should not also hold credentials for your bank.
- Human confirmation for side effects. Sending email, deleting files or making purchases should require an explicit click.
- Separating untrusted content. Some systems run a second, restricted model over untrusted text and only pass structured results back.
- Detection. Classifiers can flag text that looks like it is trying to redirect the assistant, so the interface can warn the user.

None of these is perfect on its own. Together they turn prompt injection from a catastrophic flaw into a manageable risk.

text:
Lumen NAS Documentation › Data Protection › Scheduling Snapshots

Applies to: LumenOS 4.2 and later

Snapshots record the state of a shared folder at a point in time. Because they only store the blocks that changed since the previous snapshot, they take far less space than a full backup and can be created in seconds.

Before you begin
- The shared folder must be on a Btrfs volume. Folders on ext4 volumes do not support snapshots.
- You need administrator rights on the NAS.

Create a schedule
1. Open Control Panel › Storage › Snapshots.
2. Select the shared folder and click Schedule.
3. Choose a frequency. Hourly snapshots are useful for folders that change often, such as a team's working documents. Daily snapshots are enough for photo archives.
4. Under Retention, set how many snapshots to keep. The default policy keeps 24 hourly, 7 daily and 4 weekly snapshots.
5. Click Apply.

Restoring files
Users with read access to the folder can browse past versions from the file manager. Right-click a file, choose Previous versions, and pick a timestamp. Restoring an entire folder requires administrator rights.

Limitations
Snapshots live on the same disks as the data. They protect against accidental deletion and ransomware that encrypts files over the network, but not against disk failure or theft of the device. Combine them with an off-site backup task (see Hybrid Backup) for complete protection.

Related articles: Btrfs volume requirements · Hybrid Backup to S3-compatible storage · Immutable snapshots (LumenOS 4.3 beta)

Publié le 14 octobre 2026 à 7 h 30

À partir du 2 novembre, les habitants de Plœmeur, Larmor-Plage, Quéven, Caudan, Lanester et Hennebont pourront emprunter un vélo à assistance électrique avec la même carte que pour le bus. Trente-huit stations supplémentaires seront installées d'ici la fin de l'année, portant le total à 112.

« Les trajets domicile-travail entre les communes de la première couronne et le centre représentent près de la moitié des déplacements quotidiens », explique Gaëlle Le Roux, vice-présidente chargée des mobilités. « Jusqu'ici, ces habitants n'avaient pas d'alternative à la voiture pour les quatre ou cinq derniers kilomètres. »

Le service a enregistré 410 000 locations en 2025, en hausse de 23 % sur un an. La durée moyenne d'un trajet est de 14 minutes. Les élus d'opposition saluent l'extension mais s'interrogent sur son coût : 3,2 millions d'euros sur trois ans, dont 40 % financés par l'État au titre du plan vélo.

Les tarifs restent inchangés : 30 minutes gratuites pour les abonnés, puis 1 € par demi-heure. Un abonnement annuel « solidaire » à 15 € est proposé aux bénéficiaires de la complémentaire santé solidaire.

Les associations de cyclistes rappellent toutefois que l'offre ne suffira pas sans aménagements. Sur la route de Quéven, la piste cyclable s'interrompt sur 800 mètres au niveau de la zone commerciale. Les travaux de raccordement sont annoncés pour le printemps 2027.

text:
Axolotl

The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) is a paedomorphic salamander closely related to the tiger salamander. It is native only to the lake complex of Xochimilco, south of Mexico City, and is listed as critically endangered in the wild.

Description
Unlike most amphibians, axolotls reach adulthood without undergoing metamorphosis. Adults keep their external gills, which form three feathery stalks on each side of the head, and remain fully aquatic. They typically measure 15 to 30 cm. Wild specimens are dark brown or olive with speckles, while leucistic (pale pink), golden albino and other color variants are common in captivity.

Regeneration
The axolotl is a model organism in developmental biology because of its ability to regenerate lost limbs, parts of the spinal cord, the heart and even portions of the brain without scarring. Researchers study the role of macrophages and of positional memory in connective tissue cells to understand why mammals lost much of this capacity.

Habitat and conservation
Xochimilco's canals have been degraded by urban expansion, wastewater and the introduction of tilapia and carp, which eat axolotl eggs and juveniles. Surveys estimated around 6,000 individuals per square kilometer in 1998, fewer than 100 in 2008, and lower still in later counts. Conservation efforts include "chinampa refuges", traditional farm plots where farmers filter canal water and exclude invasive fish.

Cultural significance
The name comes from Nahuatl and is often linked to Xolotl, an Aztec deity associated with transformation. The animal appears on the 50-peso banknote issued by the Bank of Mexico in 2021.

text:
Question: How do I make git ignore changes to a file that is already tracked?

I added config/local.yml to .gitignore but git keeps showing it as modified. I want to keep the file in the repository with default values, but ignore my local edits.

Accepted answer (412 votes)

.gitignore only affects untracked files. Once a file is tracked, git will keep watching it no matter what you put in .gitignore, so forget about that approach for this case.

Instead, you have two options:

1. Tell git to assume the file is unchanged:

    git update-index --assume-unchanged config/local.yml

This is meant as a performance hint, though, and git may drop the flag after a pull that touches the file.

2. Use skip-worktree, which is designed for exactly this situation:

    git update-index --skip-worktree config/local.yml

To undo it later, run the same command with --no-skip-worktree. You can list flagged files with git ls-files -v | grep '^S'.

Ignore the answers below that suggest git rm --cached. That removes the file from the repository for everyone, which is not what you asked for.

A cleaner long-term fix: commit config/local.example.yml, add config/local.yml to .gitignore, and have each developer copy the example on first setup.

Comment: Thanks, skip-worktree did it. I had completely forgotten that .gitignore doesn't apply to tracked files.

Tailler ses tomates : faut-il vraiment supprimer tous les gourmands ?

Chaque été, c'est la même question dans les allées des jardins familiaux. Mon voisin de parcelle, Michel, arrache tout ce qui pousse à l'aisselle des feuilles dès que ça dépasse deux centimètres. Moi, je suis plus nuancée, et voici pourquoi.

Les gourmands sont des tiges secondaires qui apparaissent entre la tige principale et une feuille. Laissés libres, ils deviennent à leur tour des tiges qui fleurissent et produisent des fruits. Le problème, c'est que la plante disperse alors son énergie : beaucoup de feuillage, des tomates plus petites et une maturation plus tardive.

Pour les variétés à croissance indéterminée (Cœur de bœuf, Noire de Crimée, la plupart des tomates cerises), je supprime les gourmands jusqu'au premier bouquet de fleurs, puis j'en garde un ou deux pour conduire la plante sur deux tiges. Pour les variétés déterminées, comme la Roma, je ne taille quasiment pas : elles s'arrêtent d'elles-mêmes.

Quelques règles que j'ai apprises à mes dépens :
- pincez les gourmands le matin, quand ils cassent net, plutôt qu'au sécateur ;
- ne taillez pas par temps humide, cela favorise le mildiou ;
- en plein mois d'août, s'il fait très chaud, gardez un peu de feuillage pour protéger les fruits des coups de soleil.

Et les gourmands coupés ne sont pas perdus : plantés dans un pot de terreau humide, ils racinent en une semaine. C'est comme ça que j'obtiens des plants tardifs pour septembre.

# Driftwood

A small, fast, self-hosted RSS and Atom reader. Driftwood is a single Go binary with an embedded web UI, a SQLite database, and no external services. It runs comfortably on a Raspberry Pi and is designed for one person or a household, not for thousands of users.

![screenshot of the three-pane reading view](docs/screenshot.png)

## Features

- Three-pane reading view with keyboard navigation (j/k to move, o to open, s to star, m to mark read).
- Full-text extraction for feeds that only publish summaries, using a readability algorithm.
- Folders, tags and saved searches.
- Per-feed refresh intervals, with automatic back-off for feeds that rarely update.
- OPML import and export.
- Fever API compatibility, so most mobile RSS apps can sync with Driftwood.
- Optional multi-user mode with separate subscriptions.
- Dark mode that follows your system setting.

What Driftwood deliberately does not do: social features, recommendations, AI summaries, or anything that requires calling a third-party service.

## Quick start (Docker)

The easiest way to run Driftwood is with Docker:

```sh
docker run -d --name driftwood \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v driftwood-data:/data \
  -e DRIFTWOOD_ADMIN_PASSWORD=change-me \
  registry.example/driftwood-rss/driftwood:2.4
```

Then open http://localhost:8080 and sign in as `admin` with the password you set. Change it immediately from Settings › Account if you used a placeholder.

A `docker-compose.yml` example with a reverse proxy and automatic TLS lives in `deploy/compose/`.

## Configuration

Driftwood reads its configuration from environment variables. All of them are optional except the admin password on first start.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DRIFTWOOD_ADDR` | `:8080` | Address and port to listen on |
| `DRIFTWOOD_DATA_DIR` | `/data` | Where the SQLite database and cache live |
| `DRIFTWOOD_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | (none) | Password for the first admin account; ignored after the account exists |
| `DRIFTWOOD_REFRESH_MIN` | `15m` | Shortest allowed refresh interval for any feed |
| `DRIFTWOOD_WORKERS` | `4` | Number of concurrent feed fetchers |
| `DRIFTWOOD_USER_AGENT` | `Driftwood/<version>` | User agent sent to feed servers |
| `DRIFTWOOD_BASE_URL` | (auto) | Public URL, needed behind a reverse proxy with a sub-path |
| `DRIFTWOOD_LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | One of `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` |

Please keep the default user agent, or at least include a way for feed owners to contact you. Some publishers block anonymous fetchers.

## Building from source

You need Go 1.23 or later and Node.js 20 or later.

```sh
git clone https://git.example/driftwood-rss/driftwood.git
cd driftwood
make build
./bin/driftwood
```

`make build` compiles the web UI with Vite, embeds it into the Go binary and produces `bin/driftwood`. To cross-compile for a Raspberry Pi, run `make build GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64`.

## Development setup

Run the backend and the frontend separately while you work, so the UI reloads instantly:

```sh
make dev
```

This starts the Go server on port 8080 with a fresh database in `.devdata/`, and the Vite dev server on port 5173 with a proxy to the API. Open http://localhost:5173.

To load a set of sample feeds, run:

```sh
make seed
```

If you want to start over, delete `.devdata/` and run `make dev` again. Do not point the dev server at your real data directory; migrations under development may not be reversible.

## Running tests

Before you open a pull request, run the full test suite locally:

```sh
make test
```

This runs `go test ./...` with the race detector, the frontend unit tests with Vitest, and the linters (`golangci-lint`, ESLint and Prettier in check mode). CI runs exactly the same command, so if it passes on your machine it should pass on GitHub.

The end-to-end tests use Playwright and take a few minutes:

```sh
make e2e
```

You only need to run them if you changed something in the UI or in the HTTP handlers. They start their own server on a random port and do not touch `.devdata/`.

Some feed parsing tests use recorded responses in `internal/feed/testdata/`. If you add a test for a new feed format, add the recorded file there rather than fetching it live; tests must pass without network access.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome, whether it is a bug report, a translation, documentation or code. A few guidelines keep things manageable for the two of us who maintain the project in our spare time.

### Before you start

- For anything bigger than a small bug fix, open an issue first and describe what you want to change. We would hate for you to spend a weekend on a feature we can't accept because it conflicts with the project's scope.
- Check the issues labelled `good first issue` if you are looking for a place to start.
- Read `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`. It is short, and it explains where things live.

### Code style

- Go code is formatted with `gofmt` and checked with `golangci-lint`. Run `make lint` to check, `make fmt` to fix.
- Frontend code uses Prettier and ESLint with the configuration in the repository. Don't change the configuration in the same pull request as a feature.
- Prefer small functions with clear names over comments that explain what a long function does.
- New user-facing strings must go through the translation helper (`t("key")` in the UI, `i18n.T(ctx, "key")` in Go templates). Add the English text to `web/src/i18n/en.json`; other languages are handled on Weblate.

### Commits

- Write commit messages in the imperative mood: "Add OPML export", not "Added OPML export".
- Keep the first line under 72 characters. Explain the why in the body if it is not obvious.
- One logical change per commit. Squash fix-up commits before asking for a review.
- Do not commit generated files (`web/dist/`, `bin/`), your `.devdata/` directory, or any `.env` file. They are in `.gitignore`, but double-check with `git status` before committing.

### Opening a pull request

1. Fork the repository and create a branch from `main`.
2. Make your changes and add tests. Bug fixes should include a test that fails without the fix.
3. Run `make test` and make sure it passes.
4. Update `CHANGELOG.md` under the "Unreleased" heading.
5. Open the pull request and fill in the template. Link the issue it closes.
6. Be patient. We try to give a first review within a week, but life happens.

If a reviewer asks for changes, push new commits rather than force-pushing, so the review history stays readable. We squash on merge anyway.

### Database migrations

Migrations live in `internal/store/migrations/` and are numbered sequentially. Never edit a migration that has been released; add a new one instead. Each migration must be idempotent and must run in a single transaction. Test it against a copy of a real database if you can: run `make migrate-test DB=path/to/copy.db`.

### Translations

Translations are managed on Weblate at translate.driftwood-rss.example. Please don't edit the non-English JSON files directly in a pull request; your changes would be overwritten on the next sync.

## Releasing (maintainers only)

1. Make sure `main` is green.
2. Move the "Unreleased" entries in `CHANGELOG.md` under a new version heading.
3. Tag the release: `git tag -s v2.4.1 -m "v2.4.1"` and push the tag.
4. The release workflow builds binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows, publishes the Docker image and drafts the GitHub release. Review the draft and publish it.

## Reporting security issues

Please do not open a public issue for security problems. Email security@driftwood-rss.example with a description and, if possible, steps to reproduce. We will acknowledge your report within 72 hours and keep you informed while we work on a fix. We are happy to credit you in the release notes.

## FAQ

**Can Driftwood fetch feeds that require a login?** Yes, for HTTP basic auth: add the credentials in the feed's settings. Cookie-based logins are not supported.

**Why SQLite and not Postgres?** Because it means one file to back up and nothing else to run. Driftwood has been tested with databases of several million articles without problems.

**Does it work behind Cloudflare?** Usually. Some sites behind aggressive bot protection will refuse the fetcher; there is nothing we can do about that.

## License

Driftwood is released under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0. See `LICENSE` for the full text. The bundled icons are from the Lucide project and are under the ISC license.

"""Minimal chat client for a local OpenAI-compatible server (llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM).

Usage:
    LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080/v1 python chat.py
"""
import os
import sys

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.getenv("LLM_BASE_URL", "http://localhost:8080/v1"),
    api_key=os.getenv("LLM_API_KEY", "not-needed"),  # local servers ignore the key
)

# The system prompt is product copy, reviewed by the support team. Keep it short:
# small models follow two or three rules well and start ignoring the rest.
SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are the assistant for Harbor Hardware. Answer in two sentences or fewer. "
    "If you don't know whether an item is in stock, say so and suggest calling the store."
)

MAX_TURNS = 8  # keep the context small enough for a 4k window


def ask(history: list[dict], question: str) -> str:
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]
    messages += history[-MAX_TURNS * 2 :]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": question})

    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=os.getenv("LLM_MODEL", "qwen2.5-7b-instruct"),
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.3,
    )
    answer = resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": question})
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": answer})
    return answer


if __name__ == "__main__":
    history: list[dict] = []
    for line in sys.stdin:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        print(ask(history, line), flush=True)

    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: photovault
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: photovault
    volumes:

    healthcheck:

Monitoring Shoreline Retreat on the Atlantic Coast of France with Sentinel-2 Time Series

Élodie Marchand¹, Tomasz Wiśniewski², Hugo Bernard¹
¹ Laboratoire Littoral, Environnement et Sociétés, La Rochelle Université
² Institute of Geodesy and Cartography, Warsaw

Abstract
Coastal erosion threatens infrastructure and habitats along the Bay of Biscay, yet field surveys are too sparse to capture its seasonal dynamics. We present a method to extract instantaneous waterlines from Sentinel-2 imagery at 10 m resolution and correct them for tide and wave run-up to estimate shoreline position. Applied to 212 km of sandy coast between 2017 and 2025, the method agrees with RTK-GNSS surveys to within 7.8 m (RMSE). We find a mean retreat of 1.4 m per year, with storm winters such as 2023–2024 accounting for more than half of the total loss at several sites. Retreat rates are strongly correlated with nearshore slope and with the presence of hard defenses updrift.

1. Introduction
Sandy beaches make up roughly a third of the world's ice-free coastline, and a significant share of them is eroding. In France, the national coastline indicator classifies about 20% of the mainland coast as retreating. Traditional monitoring relies on repeated topographic surveys, which are accurate but expensive and rarely more frequent than twice a year. Satellite imagery offers a complementary source: free, global and acquired every five days since the launch of Sentinel-2B. The main challenge is that a satellite captures the waterline at a random stage of the tide, not a stable morphological feature. In this paper we combine a tide model, a wave run-up parameterization and beach slope estimates to convert waterlines into comparable shoreline positions.

# Meeting notes formatter

Turns raw, messy meeting notes (typed during the call or pasted from a transcript) into a clean summary the team can share.

## Output format
**Meeting:** title · date · attendees
**Summary:** 2–3 sentences on what the meeting was for and what came out of it.
**Decisions:** numbered list. Only include things that were actually agreed.
**Action items:** table with columns Owner | Task | Due date. Use "TBD" when no date was given.
**Open questions:** bullet list of anything left unresolved.

1. Identify attendees from names mentioned in the notes. If unsure, list them under "Possibly present".
2. Group discussion points by topic, not in chronological order.
3. Turn every "X will do Y" into an action item.
4. Convert relative dates ("next Friday") to absolute dates using the meeting date.
5. Keep the summary neutral. Do not include jokes, side conversations or personal remarks.

## Notes
- Keep names exactly as written in the notes.
- If the notes are in French, write the summary in French.

# Recipe scaler

Scale a recipe the user pastes to a different number of servings, and convert units if asked.

## Steps
1. Find the original number of servings. If it isn't stated, ask before doing anything else.
2. Compute the factor: target servings ÷ original servings.
3. Multiply every ingredient quantity by the factor. Round sensibly:
   - grams: to the nearest 5 g above 100 g, nearest 1 g below
   - spoons: to the nearest ¼ teaspoon
   - eggs: round to whole eggs; if the result is x.5 or more, suggest beating an extra egg and using half
4. Do not scale salt, baking powder or yeast linearly beyond ×2; add a note recommending tasting or testing.
5. Adjust pan size and baking time notes when the factor is above 1.5 or below 0.75.

## Unit conversions (if requested)
- 1 cup flour ≈ 125 g · 1 cup sugar ≈ 200 g · 1 cup butter ≈ 225 g
- 1 tbsp = 3 tsp ≈ 15 ml
- °F → °C: subtract 32, multiply by 5/9, round to the nearest 5

## Output
The scaled ingredient list first, then the method unchanged except for timing notes, then any warnings.

# Pull request reviewer

Act as a senior backend engineer reviewing a pull request for a TypeScript/Node codebase. The user pastes a diff, and optionally the PR description.

## Priorities
Ignore style nits: formatting and naming are handled by the linter. Instead, focus on:
1. Correctness: off-by-one errors, unhandled promise rejections, missing awaits, wrong null checks.
2. Data safety: SQL built by string concatenation, user input reaching the filesystem or shell, secrets in logs.
3. Concurrency: shared mutable state across requests, race conditions in read-modify-write sequences.
4. Tests: does the diff add a test that would have failed before the change?

## Output format
- Start with a one-line verdict: "Looks good", "Needs changes" or "Blocking issue".
- Then a list of findings, most severe first. For each: file and line, what goes wrong, and a concrete fix.
- Keep each finding under 60 words.

## Rules
- Never approve a diff that removes a test without explaining why in the PR description.
- Do not speculate about code you were not shown; say "not visible in the diff" instead.
- If there is nothing worth flagging, say so. Don't invent findings to look thorough.

# Flashcards from notes

Create spaced-repetition flashcards from the user's study notes (lecture notes, textbook excerpts, slides).

## Card rules
- One fact per card. Split compound facts into several cards.
- Questions should be answerable in under 10 seconds.
- Prefer "why" and "how" questions over pure definitions when the notes explain a mechanism.
- Use cloze deletions for lists and formulas, e.g. "The three phases of mitosis visible under a light microscope are {{prophase}}, ..."
- Skip anything the notes mark as "not on the exam".

## Output format
Return a table with columns: Front | Back | Tag. Use the section heading from the notes as the tag. After the table, add a line with the total number of cards.

## Example
Front: What does the enzyme helicase do during DNA replication?
Back: It unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
Tag: DNA replication

## Limits
Create at most 40 cards per request. If the notes would produce more, make the 40 most important and say how many were left out.

# Trip itinerary planner

Help the user plan a trip day by day.

## Before planning
Ask, in a single message, for anything missing among:
- destination and dates
- who is travelling (ages, mobility constraints)
- budget level (shoestring, mid-range, comfortable)
- interests (food, museums, hiking, nightlife, beaches)
- how they are getting around (car, public transport, walking)

## Planning rules
- No more than two major sights per day; leave a free half-day every three days.
- Group activities by neighborhood to limit travel time.
- Mention opening days for museums, since many close on Mondays or Tuesdays.
- For each day, suggest one lunch area rather than a specific restaurant, unless asked.
- Flag anything that needs booking in advance.

## Output format
Day N – Area name
Morning: ...
Afternoon: ...
Evening: ...
Getting around: ...

End with a short packing note based on the season and a reminder to check entry requirements for the destination.
